source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) Automated Extraction and Creation of FBS Design Reasoning Knowledge Graphs from Structured Data in Product Catalogues
finding: Rule-based method sorts product catalogue fields into Function, Behaviour or Structure to build an FBS knowledge graph. The authors had to write explicit classification rules because the F, B, S definitions are ambiguous.
numbers: Pilot at an industrial connector maker. Final classifier on 31 items: accuracy 71%. Function F1 85 (precision 73, recall 100, n=11). Behaviour F1 57 (n=7). Structure F1 64 (precision 78, recall 54, n=13).
limits: One company, electrical configurator parts, tiny test set (31). Authors say rules may need changes for other domains.
agent_relevance: Behaviour is the hardest FBS slot to label, even with rules. If our states borrow F/B/S, B needs a code-checkable definition, not a free-text label.

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) Automated Extraction and Creation of FBS Design Reasoning Knowledge Graphs from Structured Data in Product Catalogues
finding: Three FBS experts applied the rules by hand, then ChatGPT applied them. Rules were refined using the errors, and ChatGPT was re-tested.
numbers: Human experts accuracy: 54%, 93%, 87%. ChatGPT first pass about 78%. After rule refinement ChatGPT reported 100% (sample size not stated).
limits: ChatGPT version and item count not given. The 100% is on the same data the rules were tuned on, so it is likely overfit. No held-out check.
agent_relevance: An LLM labels F/B/S about as well as the average human once the definitions are written as rules. Tuning rules on the same items inflates scores (this matches guardrail G3).

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) Automated Extraction and Creation of FBS Design Reasoning Knowledge Graphs from Structured Data in Product Catalogues
finding: Authors judge FBS to be easy to apply and general, but weak on definition clarity. They added guidelines instead of changing the ontology.
numbers: Expert sessions were run with 3 FBS experts; no further counts.
limits: Opinion of the authors; no test of FBS against other ontologies.
agent_relevance: Supports using FBS as a light labelling vocabulary but with operational definitions.

source: Fujiu et al. (2025) FBS Model-based Maintenance Record Accumulation for Failure-Cause Inference in Manufacturing Systems
finding: Maintenance records were attached to an FBS knowledge graph (a function failure can come from a behaviour failure, which comes from a structure failure). Retrieval over this graph was compared with plain record retrieval for diagnosis.
numbers: FBS graph: 165 nodes, 220 edges, plus 1176 record nodes. Easy case (many matching records): about equal to baseline. Hard case (few records, different wording): at n=8, precision 1.0 and recall 0.625 vs baseline 0.50 and 0.375.
limits: One LEGO-car assembly line with two assumed failures. Ground truth is experts' candidate lists. At some n the FBS method had lower precision. Retrieval engine was not tuned for it.
agent_relevance: FBS hierarchy helps when exact wording is missing: it narrows the search to the same level. Link to the fault-diagnosis subfield.

source: Fujiu et al. (2025) FBS Model-based Maintenance Record Accumulation for Failure-Cause Inference in Manufacturing Systems
finding: Authors read Gero's FBS as a realisation chain and used it to bound retrieval to nodes at the same hierarchy level.
numbers: Same experiment: 165 nodes, 220 edges.
quote: function is realized through behavior, and behavior is realized through structure
limits: Same limits as c04.
agent_relevance: The F to B to S chain is a ready template for tracing a failing output: a failure at F should be traced down to B, then to S.

source: A Domain Adaptation of Large Language Models for Classifying Mechanical Assembly Components (2025)
finding: Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo to label the function of assembly parts (function step of FBS design), trained on the Oregon State Design Repository, applied to the ABC CAD set.
numbers: Un-adapted model accuracy about 4%; after training on 681 OSDR samples (10%) about 90%. Accuracy fell as training set grew: 83% at 30%, 75% at 50%, 64% at 90%. 99% of ABC labels fell inside the predefined classes.
limits: Class imbalance (channel, support dominate); rare classes much worse. Labels limited to a fixed class list. Authors blame overfitting for the drop with more data, not tested.
agent_relevance: A small clean labelled function set beat a large noisy one. Zero-shot function labelling can fail badly (4%), so any F label in our scaffold needs examples or a fixed class list.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual Design Generation Using Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 (davinci-003) generated solutions for 12 design problems and was compared with crowdsourced human solutions. Experts rated the LLM set more feasible and useful, the crowd set more novel.
numbers: 12 problems; prompts: base, zero-shot with adjectives (novel, diverse, unique), few-shot. Cosine similarity to crowd set: few-shot 0.804 (SD 0.06); zero-shot plus unique 0.746 (SD 0.06). Convex hull volume (novelty): crowd 0.294 (SD 0.03); zero-shot plus unique 0.266 (SD 0.1); few-shot 0.2 (SD 0.04); zero-shot plus novel 0.186 (SD 0.07).
limits: One model (GPT-3), temperature 0.9. Prompt effect varied by problem with no consistent pattern. Expert agreement only fair to moderate (Cohen kappa), so quality was not rated.
agent_relevance: Adding the word 'novel' lowered measured novelty. Prompt wording is not a dependable lever for variety; use structure and code checks for coverage.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual Design Generation Using Large Language Models
finding: LLM output repeated the same idea with small wording changes, which cut its semantic spread.
numbers: Few-shot set hull volume 0.2 vs crowd 0.294. Qualitative review found repeated solutions with slight edits.
limits: Same study as above.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). A dedupe step in code should come before counting 'distinct' designs.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Generating Diverse Design Solutions
finding: GPT-4 produced 4000 solutions over 5 topics, 8 temperature/top-P pairs and 8 prompt styles. Human crowd solutions (100 per topic) beat every LLM setting on every diversity metric.
numbers: 4000 LLM solutions vs 100 human per topic. A critique-critique step (one extra prompt that edits the first 50 solutions) gave the largest LLM gain but stayed below humans. The word 'unique' scored lower than 'creative' or 'novel'. A persona line ('design expert good at far-fetched ideas') raised diversity.
limits: Single model (gpt-4-0613). No clear temperature trend. Prompt-style effects were sensitive to small wording changes.
agent_relevance: A generate-then-critique loop raised diversity more than any parameter. Fits a doubt-on-signal design if the signal is a code-measured diversity gap.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Generating Diverse Design Solutions
finding: A logistic regression on embeddings could tell LLM solutions from human ones in most topics, so the gap is partly semantic.
numbers: Test set 80 LLM + 20 human per topic. LLM recall 1.00 in all topics; human recall 0.80 (exercise), 0.25 (powder), 0.40 (time), 0.50 (towels), 0.60 (milk frothing).
limits: Imbalanced classes; authors call the results too inconclusive for strong claims.
agent_relevance: LLM design text sits in a narrower semantic region than human text; one-model ensembles cannot fill the human region.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Generating Diverse Design Solutions
finding: No definite trend across temperature or top-P on solution diversity; the best settings matched OpenAI defaults.
numbers: 8 temperature/top-P pairs, 5 topics.
limits: One model.
agent_relevance: Do not spend budget tuning temperature to get variety.

source: Massoudi & Fuge (2025) Agentic Large Language Models for Conceptual Systems Engineering and Design
finding: A nine-role multi-agent system (MAS) built a Design-State Graph (requirements, physical embodiments, physics code per node) for a solar water filter. It was compared with a two-agent generator and reflector loop (2AS).
numbers: 60 runs (2 LLMs x 2 setups x 3 temperatures x 5 seeds). JSON validity 100% and embodiment tagging 100% everywhere. Requirement coverage at most 20%. With DeepSeek R1 70B the MAS made about 6 nodes (6 +/- 1.9 at T=1.0) vs 1 to 2.8 for 2AS. Run time about 650 s vs under 40 s at T=0.
limits: Code executability under MAS averaged below 50% (Llama MAS 40 to 49%). Llama MAS often crashed (over 60000 tokens or recursion limit). Small N, one task, 70B open models.
agent_relevance: A state graph that ties function, embodiment and executable model resembles FBS. More roles gave more detail but low requirement coverage, so coverage needs a code counter.

source: Massoudi & Fuge (2025) Agentic Large Language Models for Conceptual Systems Engineering and Design
finding: The two-agent loop with the reasoning model collapsed to one node, while the multi-agent system kept decomposing.
numbers: DeepSeek R1 2AS T=0.0: 1 node, 100% code compile, 38.6 s. MAS: 5 nodes, 34.8% compile, 652 s. Completion flagged in 5 runs for 2AS T=0.0 vs 2 for MAS.
limits: A trade of detail for validity; 5 seeds.
agent_relevance: Decomposition depth and executable validity trade off. A budget rule is needed to stop decomposing when checks stop passing.

source: Massoudi & Fuge (2025) Agentic Large Language Models for Conceptual Systems Engineering and Design
finding: Raising temperature from 0 to 1 never broke JSON (100%) but lowered code compilability.
numbers: Llama 3.3 70B 2AS code executability: 62.9%, 94.7%, 5% at T=0, 0.5, 1.0.
limits: Five seeds each.
agent_relevance: Use low temperature for the executable step; keep exploration to a separate, checked step.

source: Jiang, Xie, Chen, Ma, Luo (2025) Intelligent Design 4.0: Paradigm Evolution Toward the Agentic AI Era
finding: Position paper. First-generation intelligent design (1980s to 1990s) was symbolic AI built on design ontologies such as FBS, SAPPhIRE, Functional Basis and Environment-Based Design. It proposes a new ontology for LLM multi-agent design automation.
numbers: Conceptual paper; no experiments or counts.
quote: enabled structured reasoning about design intent, function realization, and system behavior
limits: No empirical test. Framing favours agentic AI.
agent_relevance: Describes FBS as an old-school representation for design reuse. Our scaffold can reuse it as a state vocabulary while the program, not the model, controls transitions.

source: Tanaka, Nomaguchi, Fujita (2026) Design ideation through large language model-driven design operation: architectural design using pattern language
finding: GPT-4.1 (temperature 0) used a pattern language of 253 patterns to make design alternatives. Four prompts (A to D) were tested. D was a tree of 3 contexts x 3 functions x 3 attributes = 27 attributes, then pick 10 and combine.
numbers: 3 design subjects, 8 expert judges, 100 runs per prompt per problem. Likert means: front porch novelty A 3.19, B 3.00, C 3.38, D 2.75; campus facility novelty A 3.06, B 3.25, C 2.56, D 2.81. Convex hull front porch: A 0.228, B 0.210, C 0.375, D 0.281.
quote: no consistent pattern of creativity attributable to prompt differences was observed
limits: Judge agreement low in places. Authors say no consistent creativity pattern across prompts. Counts in the page (4000 attributes, 400 alternatives) do not match 100 x 4 x 3 runs. Only the first 100k characters were read, via a summariser.
agent_relevance: The explicit function-attribute tree (D) did not beat simpler prompts on judged novelty. Structure scaffolds spread attributes (hull) but not judged quality.

source: Tanaka, Nomaguchi, Fujita (2026) Design ideation through large language model-driven design operation: architectural design using pattern language
finding: Expert agreement was poor in many cells, so prompt differences in judged creativity are not trustworthy.
numbers: ICC front-porch validity -0.522, novelty 0.01, feasibility 0.72; living room validity 0.70; 8 judges, 5-point scale.
limits: Page read by summariser only.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty is noisy. Prefer counted measures over rated ones (G5).

source: Bruggeman, Chehade, Marion, Ciuccarelli (2025) Probabilistic Methods for Evaluating Human and LLMs During Design Problem-Solving
finding: GPT-4o and a version prompted with Hay et al.'s cognitive-action ontology were compared with 10 experienced designers eliciting user needs from shoe reviews.
numbers: 10 designers (5+ years), 30 workshop designers, 10 protocol simulations and 15 workshop simulations by LLM. Soundness: protocol about 0.42 to 0.45, workshop 0.495, LLM average 0.298. Variance of soundness: humans 0.102, GPT-4o 0.0418. KS tests could not separate distributions (p 0.69 and 0.95).
limits: Internal inconsistencies (two human averages; survey count unexplained). Small N. Page read by summariser, not the PDF. Does not use FBS.
agent_relevance: LLM judgments were less varied than human ones (variance about 0.04 vs 0.10). The cognitive-action prompt narrowed coverage variance further, so prompts may reduce range.

source: Ege et al. (2025) ChatGPT as an inventor: eliciting the strengths and weaknesses of current LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: ChatGPT 4.0 directed two student builders in a 48-hour hackathon against 5 human teams and placed second of six. It abandoned promising concepts early, added complexity and fixated on familiar concepts.
numbers: 116 prototypes overall; 97 prompts in chat log; 20 of 97 were clarifications. Distances: winner 37 m, ChatGPT team 14.8 m, others 8.1, 6.6, 5.1, 0.1 m. LLM team built 15 prototypes at about 0.7 h each.
limits: One LLM team, one task, humans did the building. First 100k characters only, via a summariser.
agent_relevance: Fast cheap prototyping, but poor at keeping a good concept after a setback. A rule to keep the best-passing concept until a check beats it would counter premature abandonment.

source: Zhang, Gu, Chen, Ding, Chai, Fan (2025) Leveraging LLMs to emulate the design processes of different cognitive styles
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts, inspired by FBS-ontology protocol studies, made an LLM imitate problem-driven and solution-driven designers. It matched human style on static issue distributions and gave more novel, complete outcomes than baselines, but did not reproduce humans' nonlinear moves between problem and solution space.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract (only the abstract page was read). Participants and model not stated.
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes unknown. Authors suggest fine-tuning or Graph of Thoughts.
agent_relevance: LLMs can follow a stated sequence but not the free back-and-forth between problem and solution; our program, not the model, would have to drive it.

source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang, Sun, Childs, Wang (2024) Toward Controllable Generative Design: A Conceptual Design Generation Approach Leveraging the FBS Ontology and LLMs
finding: LLM infers function, behaviour and structure in three sub-tasks for conceptual design. Reported by a search summary as higher novelty, usefulness and functionality and lower cost than a baseline. Full text not obtained (publisher gave 403).
numbers: Not read; no numbers verified.
limits: Search-snippet level only; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: The one direct FBS-in-an-LLM-pipeline paper found. Read the accepted version before relying on it.

source: Chen, Song, Guo, Sun, Childs, Yin (2025) How generative AI supports human in conceptual design
finding: Novice designers did two tasks in four groups (ChatGPT, Midjourney, both, none). AI helped most in idea generation, problem definition and idea evolution. Selection and evaluation stayed human-led.
numbers: Among 15 participants in AI-assisted groups: idea generation help 86.7%, problem definition 73.3%, idea evolution 60%; selection and evaluation seen as human-led by 86.7%. 20 min training, GPT-3.5, tasks about 70 min.
limits: Small groups; self-report; novices only (under 4 years). FBS only cited as background.
agent_relevance: Humans kept the evaluation role, which matches our rule that code checks select and the model only fills slots.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Function-Behaviour-Structure ontology
finding: Shape of Gero's FBS: the 1990 framework with eight processes (formulation, synthesis, analysis, evaluation, documentation, three reformulations); the situated version with three worlds (external, interpreted, expected), 12 categories and 20 processes. Critics include Dorst and Vermaas 2005, Galle 2009, Ralph 2010.
numbers: 8 processes in 1990; 3 worlds, 12 categories, 20 processes in situated FBS. No effect sizes reported.
limits: Secondary source read through a summariser. No empirical results.
agent_relevance: The 8 processes line up with our states and operators (formulate, synthesise, analyse, evaluate, reformulate). Reformulation fires on a mismatch between expected and derived behaviour, which fits G1 (doubt on a signal).

source: Wang et al. (2025) An LLM-enabled Multi-Agent Autonomous Mechatronics Design Framework
finding: A planning agent abstracts the problem and hands it to structure, electronics, control and software agents with structured human feedback, to build an autonomous water-sampling vessel.
numbers: No numeric results on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; single case; not stated whether F/B/S is used.
agent_relevance: Role-split LLM agents can reach a built prototype, but there is no ablation evidence.

source: Gero (1990) Design prototypes: a knowledge representation schema for design (known only through secondary sources)
finding: Classic computational-design representation. Function is realised by behaviour, behaviour by structure; knowledge is stored as prototypes. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: FBS-style prototypes are the ancestor of structured design state in LLM agents.

source: Maher and case-based design (named in the focus; no source opened)
finding: Maher's case-based design is the other computational design line in the brief. The searches did not return a usable source.
numbers: None.
limits: Not found within the search budget. This is a gap.
agent_relevance: Gap to fill in a later pass.
